items.title: Recent Advances in AI Are Creating a ‘Paradigm Shift’ for Robotics | Research UC Berkeley
items.summary:
In recent months, artificial intelligence agents that can reason, plan and use external tools to accomplish multistep tasks have already reshaped computer coding, online shopping, dinner reservations and cyberattacks.

Robotics might be next.

Ken Goldberg, a UC Berkeley roboticist and professor of engineering, said new models make it possible for teams of AI agents to develop robot-control programs, test them in simulated environments and revise the code when something doesn’t work. [...] Then, AI agents generate and connect these skills into a robot program. Using NVIDIA’s Isaac simulation libraries, the agents autonomously rehearse the program across task variations, identify where failures happen and refine the approach before deployment. [...] OpenAI’s recent release of its Astra model made the process even more promising, Goldberg said. His postdoctoral students Eric Kaiyuan Chen and Shuangyu Xie gave Astra access to their simulation interface and a short video of a real robot whose assignment was using a sponge to wipe ink off a metal bar. In less than an hour, the AI tool created and fine-tuned a physics simulation that accurately reproduced the video, including very realistic deformations of the sponge.

items.title: Google AI policy forces decision for San Diego schools – NBC 7 San Diego
items.summary:
As districts consider their options, students are already seeing artificial intelligence become a more common part of everyday learning.

“I feel like I see a lot of people using AI now,” said Delilah Ortiz, a student at El Camino High School.

Some students believe the focus should be on establishing guidelines for AI use rather than banning the technology entirely. [...] San Diego County school districts face a January deadline to decide whether to opt in to Google's artificial intelligence features or lose access to the company's search engine, forcing educators to weigh the benefits of AI against concerns about student access to the technology. [...] Google plans to disable a range of AI-powered features, including Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Search in January to give school districts more control over the technology students can access. However, districts that want to continue using Google Search will have to opt in to the AI features.

The previously undisclosed incident occurred June 18, when Switzerland faced Bosnia and Herzegovina at SoFi Stadium outside Los Angeles, Army Capt. The GenAI Task Force travels around the globe to sit down with troops on operations floors and in the field and find AI fixes for their most pressing problems.

turns.assistant_text:
Here are some theories and concepts related to machine learning (ML):

### Research Papers on Machine Learning Theories

1. **[Generalizing Machine Learning Evaluation through the Integration of Shannon Entropy and Rough Set Theory](http://arxiv.org/abs/2404.12511v1)**  
   This paper explores the integration of Shannon entropy and rough set theory to enhance the evaluation of machine learning models. It proposes a framework that combines the granularity of rough set theory with the uncertainty quantification of Shannon entropy, providing insights into data complexity and model robustness.  
   - Authors: Olga Cherednichenko, Dmytro Chernyshov, Dmytro Sytnikov, Polina Sytnikova  
   - [PDF Link](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.12511v1)

2. **[Emotion in Reinforcement Learning Agents and Robots: A Survey](http://arxiv.org/abs/1705.05172v1)**  
   This survey discusses computational models of emotion in reinforcement learning agents, focusing on how emotions influence decision-making and learning efficiency. It provides insights into the integration of emotion theory with reinforcement learning.  
   - Authors: Thomas M. Moerland, Joost Broekens, Catholijn M. Jonker  
   - [PDF Link](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.05172v1)

3. **[Explanatory Machine Learning for Sequential Human Teaching](http://arxiv.org/abs/2205.10250v2)**  
   This paper examines the comprehensibility of machine-learned theories and how the ordering of concept presentations affects human understanding. It proposes a framework for sequential teaching that enhances comprehension.  
   - Authors: Lun Ai, Johannes Langer, Stephen H. Muggleton, Ute Schmid  
   - [PDF Link](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.10250v2)

4. **[On-Device Machine Learning: An Algorithms and Learning Theory Perspective](http://arxiv.org/abs/1911.00623v2)**  
   This survey discusses the challenges and future directions of on-device learning, reformulating it as resource-constrained learning. It covers various topics related to machine learning algorithms and their application on devices.  
   - Authors: Sauptik Dhar, Junyao Guo, Jiayi Liu, Samarth Tripathi, Unmesh Kurup, Mohak Shah  
   - [PDF Link](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.00623v2)

5. **[Why Interpretability in Machine Learning? An Answer Using Distributed Detection and Data Fusion Theory](http://arxiv.org/abs/1806.09710v1)**  
   This paper argues for the importance of interpretability in machine learning models, using the theory of distributed detection to characterize the performance of systems that combine human interpretation with machine learning outputs.  
   - Authors: Kush R. Varshney, Prashant Khanduri, Pranay Sharma, Shan Zhang, Pramod K. Varshney  
   - [PDF Link](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.09710v1)

### General Resources on Machine Learning Theories

1. **[The End of AI Frontiers – Machine Learning (Theory)](https://hunch.net?p=13764006)**  
   A discussion on machine learning and learning theory research, exploring the boundaries of AI.

2. **[Diving into Deep Learning - Theory and Applications with PyTorch](https://www.sib.swiss/training/course/20261203_DEEPP)**  
   A course that covers the theoretical foundations and applications of deep learning in various fields.

3. **[Machine Learning | Data Science, Algorithms & Automation | Britannica](https://www.britannica.com/technology/machine-learning)**  
   An overview of machine learning, its applications, and the algorithms involved.

4. **[Learning Theory - Recent articles and discoveries | Springer Nature Link](https://link.springer.com/subjects/learning-theory)**  
   A collection of recent articles and discoveries in learning theory, covering various aspects of machine learning.

These resources should provide a solid foundation for understanding various theories in machine learning. If you need more specific information or additional topics, feel free to ask!

items.title: Generalizing Machine Learning Evaluation through the Integration of Shannon Entropy and Rough Set Theory
items.summary: This research paper delves into the innovative integration of Shannon entropy and rough set theory, presenting a novel approach to generalize the evaluation approach in machine learning. The conventional application of entropy, primarily focused on information uncertainty, is extended through its combination with rough set theory to offer a deeper insight into data's intrinsic structure and the interpretability of machine learning models. We introduce a comprehensive framework that synergizes the granularity of rough set theory with the uncertainty quantification of Shannon entropy, applied across a spectrum of machine learning algorithms. Our methodology is rigorously tested on various datasets, showcasing its capability to not only assess predictive performance but also to illuminate the underlying data complexity and model robustness. The results underscore the utility of this integrated approach in enhancing the evaluation landscape of machine learning, offering a multi-faceted perspective that balances accuracy with a profound understanding of data attributes and model dynamics. This paper contributes a groundbreaking perspective to machine learning evaluation, proposing a method that encapsulates a holistic view of model performance, thereby facilitating more informed decision-making in model selection and application.

items.title: Emotion in Reinforcement Learning Agents and Robots: A Survey
items.summary: This article provides the first survey of computational models of emotion in reinforcement learning (RL) agents. The survey focuses on agent/robot emotions, and mostly ignores human user emotions. Emotions are recognized as functional in decision-making by influencing motivation and action selection. Therefore, computational emotion models are usually grounded in the agent's decision making architecture, of which RL is an important subclass. Studying emotions in RL-based agents is useful for three research fields. For machine learning (ML) researchers, emotion models may improve learning efficiency. For the interactive ML and human-robot interaction (HRI) community, emotions can communicate state and enhance user investment. Lastly, it allows affective modelling (AM) researchers to investigate their emotion theories in a successful AI agent class. This survey provides background on emotion theory and RL. It systematically addresses 1) from what underlying dimensions (e.g., homeostasis, appraisal) emotions can be derived and how these can be modelled in RL-agents, 2) what types of emotions have been derived from these dimensions, and 3) how these emotions may either influence the learning efficiency of the agent or be useful as social signals. We also systematically compare evaluation criteria, and draw connections to important RL sub-domains like (intrinsic) motivation and model-based RL. In short, this survey provides both a practical overview for engineers wanting to implement emotions in their RL agents, and identifies challenges and directions for future emotion-RL research.

items.title: Explanatory machine learning for sequential human teaching
items.summary: The topic of comprehensibility of machine-learned theories has recently drawn increasing attention. Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) uses logic programming to derive logic theories from small data based on abduction and induction techniques. Learned theories are represented in the form of rules as declarative descriptions of obtained knowledge. In earlier work, the authors provided the first evidence of a measurable increase in human comprehension based on machine-learned logic rules for simple classification tasks. In a later study, it was found that the presentation of machine-learned explanations to humans can produce both beneficial and harmful effects in the context of game learning. We continue our investigation of comprehensibility by examining the effects of the ordering of concept presentations on human comprehension. In this work, we examine the explanatory effects of curriculum order and the presence of machine-learned explanations for sequential problem-solving. We show that 1) there exist tasks A and B such that learning A before B has a better human comprehension with respect to learning B before A and 2) there exist tasks A and B such that the presence of explanations when learning A contributes to improved human comprehension when subsequently learning B. We propose a framework for the effects of sequential teaching on comprehension based on an existing definition of comprehensibility and provide evidence for support from data collected in human trials. Empirical results show that sequential teaching of concepts with increasing complexity a) has a beneficial effect on human comprehension and b) leads to human re-discovery of divide-and-conquer problem-solving strategies, and c) studying machine-learned explanations allows adaptations of human problem-solving strategy with better performance.

items.title: On-Device Machine Learning: An Algorithms and Learning Theory Perspective
items.summary: The predominant paradigm for using machine learning models on a device is to train a model in the cloud and perform inference using the trained model on the device. However, with increasing number of smart devices and improved hardware, there is interest in performing model training on the device. Given this surge in interest, a comprehensive survey of the field from a device-agnostic perspective sets the stage for both understanding the state-of-the-art and for identifying open challenges and future avenues of research. However, on-device learning is an expansive field with connections to a large number of related topics in AI and machine learning (including online learning, model adaptation, one/few-shot learning, etc.). Hence, covering such a large number of topics in a single survey is impractical. This survey finds a middle ground by reformulating the problem of on-device learning as resource constrained learning where the resources are compute and memory. This reformulation allows tools, techniques, and algorithms from a wide variety of research areas to be compared equitably. In addition to summarizing the state-of-the-art, the survey also identifies a number of challenges and next steps for both the algorithmic and theoretical aspects of on-device learning.

items.title: Why Interpretability in Machine Learning? An Answer Using Distributed Detection and Data Fusion Theory
items.summary: As artificial intelligence is increasingly affecting all parts of society and life, there is growing recognition that human interpretability of machine learning models is important. It is often argued that accuracy or other similar generalization performance metrics must be sacrificed in order to gain interpretability. Such arguments, however, fail to acknowledge that the overall decision-making system is composed of two entities: the learned model and a human who fuses together model outputs with his or her own information. As such, the relevant performance criteria should be for the entire system, not just for the machine learning component. In this work, we characterize the performance of such two-node tandem data fusion systems using the theory of distributed detection. In doing so, we work in the population setting and model interpretable learned models as multi-level quantizers. We prove that under our abstraction, the overall system of a human with an interpretable classifier outperforms one with a black box classifier.

   - Authors: Sauptik Dhar, Junyao Guo, Jiayi Liu, Samarth Tripathi, Unmesh Kurup, Mohak Shah  
   - [PDF Link](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.00623v2)

5. **[Why Interpretability in Machine Learning? An Answer Using Distributed Detection and Data Fusion Theory](http://arxiv.org/abs/1806.09710v1)**  
   This paper argues for the importance of interpretability in machine learning models, using the theory of distributed detection to characterize the performance of systems that combine human interpretation with machine learning outputs.  
   - Authors: Kush R. Varshney, Prashant Khanduri, Pranay Sharma, Shan Zhang, Pramod K. Varshney  
   - [PDF Link](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.09710v1)

### General Resources on Machine Learning Theories

1. **[The End of AI Frontiers – Machine Learning (Theory)](https://hunch.net?p=13764006)**  
   A discussion on machine learning and learning theory research, exploring the boundaries of AI.

2. **[Diving into Deep Learning - Theory and Applications with PyTorch](https://www.sib.swiss/training/course/20261203_DEEPP)**  
   A course that covers the theoretical foundations and applications of deep learning in various fields.

3. **[Machine Learning | Data Science, Algorithms & Automation | Britannica](https://www.britannica.com/technology/machine-learning)**  
   An overview of machine learning, its applications, and the algorithms involved.

4. **[Learning Theory - Recent articles and discoveries | Springer Nature Link](https://link.springer.com/subjects/learning-theory)**  
   A collection of recent articles and discoveries in learning theory, covering various aspects of machine learning.

These resources should provide a solid foundation for understanding various theories in machine learning. If you need more specific information or additional topics, feel free to ask!

items.title: Generalizing Machine Learning Evaluation through the Integration of Shannon Entropy and Rough Set Theory
items.summary: This research paper delves into the innovative integration of Shannon entropy and rough set theory, presenting a novel approach to generalize the evaluation approach in machine learning. The conventional application of entropy, primarily focused on information uncertainty, is extended through its combination with rough set theory to offer a deeper insight into data's intrinsic structure and the interpretability of machine learning models. We introduce a comprehensive framework that synergizes the granularity of rough set theory with the uncertainty quantification of Shannon entropy, applied across a spectrum of machine learning algorithms. Our methodology is rigorously tested on various datasets, showcasing its capability to not only assess predictive performance but also to illuminate the underlying data complexity and model robustness. The results underscore the utility of this integrated approach in enhancing the evaluation landscape of machine learning, offering a multi-faceted perspective that balances accuracy with a profound understanding of data attributes and model dynamics. This paper contributes a groundbreaking perspective to machine learning evaluation, proposing a method that encapsulates a holistic view of model performance, thereby facilitating more informed decision-making in model selection and application.

items.title: Emotion in Reinforcement Learning Agents and Robots: A Survey
items.summary: This article provides the first survey of computational models of emotion in reinforcement learning (RL) agents. The survey focuses on agent/robot emotions, and mostly ignores human user emotions. Emotions are recognized as functional in decision-making by influencing motivation and action selection. Therefore, computational emotion models are usually grounded in the agent's decision making architecture, of which RL is an important subclass. Studying emotions in RL-based agents is useful for three research fields. For machine learning (ML) researchers, emotion models may improve learning efficiency. For the interactive ML and human-robot interaction (HRI) community, emotions can communicate state and enhance user investment. Lastly, it allows affective modelling (AM) researchers to investigate their emotion theories in a successful AI agent class. This survey provides background on emotion theory and RL. It systematically addresses 1) from what underlying dimensions (e.g., homeostasis, appraisal) emotions can be derived and how these can be modelled in RL-agents, 2) what types of emotions have been derived from these dimensions, and 3) how these emotions may either influence the learning efficiency of the agent or be useful as social signals. We also systematically compare evaluation criteria, and draw connections to important RL sub-domains like (intrinsic) motivation and model-based RL. In short, this survey provides both a practical overview for engineers wanting to implement emotions in their RL agents, and identifies challenges and directions for future emotion-RL research.

items.title: Explanatory machine learning for sequential human teaching
items.summary: The topic of comprehensibility of machine-learned theories has recently drawn increasing attention. Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) uses logic programming to derive logic theories from small data based on abduction and induction techniques. Learned theories are represented in the form of rules as declarative descriptions of obtained knowledge. In earlier work, the authors provided the first evidence of a measurable increase in human comprehension based on machine-learned logic rules for simple classification tasks. In a later study, it was found that the presentation of machine-learned explanations to humans can produce both beneficial and harmful effects in the context of game learning. We continue our investigation of comprehensibility by examining the effects of the ordering of concept presentations on human comprehension. In this work, we examine the explanatory effects of curriculum order and the presence of machine-learned explanations for sequential problem-solving. We show that 1) there exist tasks A and B such that learning A before B has a better human comprehension with respect to learning B before A and 2) there exist tasks A and B such that the presence of explanations when learning A contributes to improved human comprehension when subsequently learning B. We propose a framework for the effects of sequential teaching on comprehension based on an existing definition of comprehensibility and provide evidence for support from data collected in human trials. Empirical results show that sequential teaching of concepts with increasing complexity a) has a beneficial effect on human comprehension and b) leads to human re-discovery of divide-and-conquer problem-solving strategies, and c) studying machine-learned explanations allows adaptations of human problem-solving strategy with better performance.

items.title: On-Device Machine Learning: An Algorithms and Learning Theory Perspective
items.summary: The predominant paradigm for using machine learning models on a device is to train a model in the cloud and perform inference using the trained model on the device. However, with increasing number of smart devices and improved hardware, there is interest in performing model training on the device. Given this surge in interest, a comprehensive survey of the field from a device-agnostic perspective sets the stage for both understanding the state-of-the-art and for identifying open challenges and future avenues of research. However, on-device learning is an expansive field with connections to a large number of related topics in AI and machine learning (including online learning, model adaptation, one/few-shot learning, etc.). Hence, covering such a large number of topics in a single survey is impractical. This survey finds a middle ground by reformulating the problem of on-device learning as resource constrained learning where the resources are compute and memory. This reformulation allows tools, techniques, and algorithms from a wide variety of research areas to be compared equitably. In addition to summarizing the state-of-the-art, the survey also identifies a number of challenges and next steps for both the algorithmic and theoretical aspects of on-device learning.

items.title: Why Interpretability in Machine Learning? An Answer Using Distributed Detection and Data Fusion Theory
items.summary: As artificial intelligence is increasingly affecting all parts of society and life, there is growing recognition that human interpretability of machine learning models is important. It is often argued that accuracy or other similar generalization performance metrics must be sacrificed in order to gain interpretability. Such arguments, however, fail to acknowledge that the overall decision-making system is composed of two entities: the learned model and a human who fuses together model outputs with his or her own information. As such, the relevant performance criteria should be for the entire system, not just for the machine learning component. In this work, we characterize the performance of such two-node tandem data fusion systems using the theory of distributed detection. In doing so, we work in the population setting and model interpretable learned models as multi-level quantizers. We prove that under our abstraction, the overall system of a human with an interpretable classifier outperforms one with a black box classifier.
